acknowledge.text: You're tired. Rest is a real need.

options.title: Rest, even briefly
options.text: Sit or lie down, close your eyes, and let your body be heavy for a while.
options.why: A short rest can help when energy is low.

options.title: The basics
options.text: Water, something to eat, a bit of daylight: pick one.
options.why: Small basics can often lift tiredness a little.

acknowledge.text: Nothing is grabbing you right now.

options.title: Try something new and small
options.text: Learn one new thing, or go somewhere slightly different.
options.why: Novelty, even small, can help a flat day.

options.title: Is it rest in disguise?
options.text: Is part of you asking for a break, rather than more to do?
options.why: Boredom can sometimes be tiredness in another form.

acknowledge.text: Something did not turn out as you hoped. That hurts.

options.title: Say what you hoped for
options.text: What did you hope would happen?
options.why: Naming the hope can help you grieve it, and find what still matters.

options.title: Kind words
options.text: What would you say to a friend who felt this disappointment?
options.why: Kindness towards yourself can make disappointment easier to carry.
options.prompt: What I'd say to a friend:

acknowledge.text: It is hard to get going. That happens.

options.title: The tiniest start
options.text: Choose a version so small it feels almost silly, and do just that.
options.why: A tiny start often makes the next step easier.

options.title: Is something in the way?
options.text: Are you tired, unsure, or not keen on this? Any answer is fine.
options.why: Knowing what is in the way can help you choose what to do next.

acknowledge.text: You feel shy right now. That is gentle, and okay.

options.title: Go at your own pace
options.text: It is okay to take your time before joining in.
options.why: Giving yourself time often makes stepping forward easier.

options.title: One person
options.text: Talk to one person you feel comfortable with.
options.why: One familiar face can make a room feel smaller.

acknowledge.text: Not much feels like it matters right now. That's hard to sit with.

options.title: Look after the basics
options.text: Water, food, daylight, a little movement: pick one.
options.why: Low energy often eases a little when the body is cared for.

options.title: Small contact
options.text: Send one short message to someone you like.
options.why: A small connection can sometimes bring a flicker back.

acknowledge.text: You're losing heart. That's a hard place to be.

options.title: What have you already done?
options.text: Write down the steps you have already taken, however small.
options.why: Seeing progress written down can help when it feels like nothing is moving.

options.title: Make it smaller
options.text: What is a smaller goal you could manage this week?
options.why: A smaller step can feel possible again.
options.prompt: A smaller goal for this week:

acknowledge.text: You feel like you have little strength right now. Be gentle with yourself.

options.title: Rest and refuel
options.text: Sit somewhere comfortable, have a drink of water or a snack.
options.why: Looking after your body can give you a little more to work with.

options.title: Strength looks different
options.text: What have you managed today, even if it doesn't seem like much?
options.why: Strength often shows up in small things we overlook.

acknowledge.text: You feel drained. Running on empty is hard.

options.title: Stop for a moment
options.text: If you can, pause everything and rest for a little while.
options.why: Even a short stop can help when you are running on empty.

options.title: What is draining you?
options.text: Is there one thing you could do less of, or ask for help with?
options.why: Spotting a drain can help you protect your energy.

acknowledge.text: You've been going along with things. It might be worth checking in with yourself.

options.title: What do you want?
options.text: If it were up to you, what would you choose?
options.why: Noticing your own wishes can help you speak up when it matters.

options.title: Practise the words
options.text: Write one sentence you could say to ask for what you need.
options.why: Rehearsing words can make them easier to say.
options.prompt: A sentence to ask for what I need:

acknowledge.text: Loneliness is a hard feeling. Reaching for connection is a good instinct.

options.title: One small message
options.text: Send a short message to someone, even just "thinking of you".
options.why: A small connection can ease loneliness a little.

options.title: Be around people
options.text: Go somewhere with people, like a café or a park, even without talking.
options.why: Being near others can help, even quietly.

acknowledge.text: Something has hurt you. That deserves care.

options.title: Name what happened
options.text: What hurt? Write it in your own words.
options.why: Putting hurt into words can make it a little easier to hold.

options.title: Comfort, on purpose
options.text: Something warm and familiar: a blanket, a drink, a favourite song.
options.why: Choosing comfort is a way of being on your own side.

acknowledge.text: Guilt is heavy. It often means you care about doing right.

options.title: What can you do now?
options.text: Is there something you could do to make it right, or a lesson to keep?
options.why: Guilt can often ease when it turns into a step or a lesson.
options.prompt: What I can do now, or take from this:

options.title: Kindness too
options.text: What would you say to a friend who felt this guilt?
options.why: Being kind to yourself can sit alongside taking responsibility.
options.prompt: What I'd say to a friend:

acknowledge.text: Feeling rejected hurts. It says nothing final about your worth.

options.title: Someone who values you
options.text: Reach out to someone who you know cares about you.
options.why: Connection with people who value you can soften rejection.

options.title: Remember what is true
options.text: Write down three things people appreciate about you.
options.why: Remembering your strengths can help after a rejection.
options.prompt: Three things people appreciate about me:

acknowledge.text: You're comparing yourself and coming up short. That's hard to carry.

options.title: Your own path
options.text: What have you grown in, compared with yourself a year ago?
options.why: Comparing with your past self is often fairer and kinder.

options.title: A letter for this
options.text: Write to yourself for the next time you feel this way.
options.why: Your own kind words can be easier to trust later.

acknowledge.text: You feel like you're not enough. That feeling is not the whole truth.

options.title: Evidence for you
options.text: Write three things you have done that took effort or care.
options.why: Seeing evidence of your effort can quieten the not-enough feeling.
options.prompt: Three things I've done with effort or care:

options.title: A friend's view
options.text: What would a friend who knows you well say about you?
options.why: Borrowing a kinder view can help you see yourself more fairly.
options.prompt: What a good friend would say about me:

acknowledge.text: You feel small and unseen right now. You matter more than this feeling says.

options.title: Reach someone
options.text: Send a message to someone who knows you.
options.why: Being seen by one person can make a big difference.

options.title: Talk to someone
options.text: If this feeling is heavy, you can talk to someone now.
options.why: You deserve support, and you do not have to earn it.

acknowledge.text: You feel stupid about something. That's a harsh word to carry; let's soften it.

options.title: Swap the word
options.text: Is "I made a mistake" or "I didn't know" more accurate?
options.why: A fairer word can make a hard moment easier to learn from.

options.title: Talk to yourself like a friend
options.text: What would you say to a friend who said this about themselves?
options.why: Many people are much kinder to friends than to themselves.
options.prompt: What I'd say to a friend:

acknowledge.text: This is one of the heaviest feelings to carry. You deserve kindness right now.

options.title: Slow breathing
options.text: A few slow breaths before anything else.
options.why: Steadying the body can make room for gentler thoughts.

options.title: Talk to someone
options.text: If it feels heavy, talk to someone you trust, or a support line.
options.why: Feelings like this often ease a little when they are shared safely.

acknowledge.text: Feeling numb can be the mind's way of taking a break. It doesn't have to be fixed right now.

options.title: Notice five things
options.text: Gently notice five things you can see.
options.why: Gentle attention to your surroundings can help you feel a little more present.

options.title: Talk to someone
options.text: If the numbness has been here a while, talking to someone can help.
options.why: You do not have to work this out alone.

acknowledge.text: It feels like nothing you do will help. That's very hard. You don't have to solve it right now.

options.title: Just breathe
options.text: Follow the circle for a few rounds. Nothing else.
options.why: Steady breathing can give you a moment of steadiness.

options.title: Talk to someone now
options.text: You do not have to carry this alone. People can listen, any time.
options.why: Support can help when things feel out of your hands.

acknowledge.text: Things feel really hard right now. Let's keep everything small and gentle.

options.title: Comfort first
options.text: A warm drink, a blanket, a familiar sound. Something that has helped before.
options.why: Comfort on purpose can help a little when things are very hard.

options.title: Talk to someone
options.text: If it feels too heavy, reach out to someone you trust, or a support line.
options.why: You deserve support, right now.

acknowledge.text: This is a very heavy feeling. You do not have to deal with it alone.

options.title: One small thing for your body
options.text: Water, a bite to eat, or a few slow breaths. Just one.
options.why: Small acts of care can help when everything feels heavy.

options.title: Talk to someone
options.text: Talking to someone you trust, or a support line, can help. If this feeling has been around for a while, a doctor can help too.
options.why: Support is there for exactly this, and you deserve it.
